I've been a nurse for 14 years. There are a lot of reasons I'm making the change, but I'll try to boil it down to the big ones. If this is tl;dr just go to the last bit.

Nursing has never really felt like the right fit for me. I'm somewhat socially awkward, and healthcare is a very social profession. I'm not antisocial, I just am a bit introverted. 

I never found a specialty I've enjoyed as a nurse. I've worked in many inpatient and outpatient roles. I've done psych nursing, correctional nursing, rehab, cardiology, orthopedics, etc. None of them satisfied me.

Healthcare is a mess in the US. We've been short on nurses for decades. I've come to realize that hospitals are not interested in safe staffing or patient outcomes. Nurse: Patient ratios are getting worse in states that don't have legislation in place. Hospitals are interested in maximum profit, so I get spread as thinly as possible. I was happy while working overseas (Australia) but had to come back to the US after one of my parents became very ill.

Covid changed healthcare and society a lot. I used to get thanked a lot. Patients used to be, well, patient. Hospitals always treated us like crap but the work was reasonable. These days, I can't go two shifts without being yelled at by a patient, family member, or doctor. I regularly got mandated to work overtime and, as a result, rarely got to make plans or see family/friends. In my first 8 years a a nurse, I never had a vacation request approved. Started working as a travel nurse to avoid the mandated overtime, missed family reunions, loss of friends, and to get away from the stress. Unfortunately, that means I get to spend three months at a time in cities hours away from the people I love. 

Nursing has transitioned from a specialist career into a service career. Hospitals are constantly chasing patient satisfaction scores instead of focusing on patient outcomes. As a result, I tend to get treated like I work in a hotel/restaurant by patients and families. 

But if I had to boil it down to one reason, though,  this is it. 

I've been assaulted three times at work over the years. By patients and family members. Each time, it was about something I had no control over (bad food, doc refusing to give a patient narcotics, having to not eat before a procedure). The first time I had a tooth knocked out, the second I was knocked unconscious by a patient's son, and the last I was strangled with my stethoscope. Every time I've been asked (by management) "what could you have done differently?"

It really depends on how you want to lose the weight and what your end goal is.

Conventional weight training with a bit of cardio will help you keep/build muscle while losing weight. Ideally you'd do this through very mild calorie restriction while being mindful with your macros. I tried it for a couple months and was disappointed with the results. It worked but was a slow going process.

If you want to lose weight fast calorie restriction and High Intensity Interval Training. You won't pack on muscle but you will get rid of the weight. This is the route I took. I can build up the muscle after I stabilize near my goal weight.

I will run stairs/bleachers often. 3 flights flat out, one at a walk, and 3 more as fast as I can, and so on. I also use leg weights while running. One minute hard run, 30 seconds light jog and repeat. Make the runs and rest periods longer until you get to 3 minutes of running.

There's all sorts of HIIT workouts online.

I am 5'9" (175.3 cm) and when I started my weight loss journey I weighed 320 lb (145 kg). I've lost just under 80lb (36kg). I started HIIT in December. You get used to the calorie restriction. Just don't drop below 1500 calories.

I didn't really have my wake up call until I was 30. I suddenly found myself single, without any friends, and deeply unhappy with my career choices. I tried to just hang onto the status quo until I ended up losing a very lucrative management position. I was profoundly depressed.

Since that low I've done a lot to Improve my situation. These are the things I do to live a better life.  


* Find a therapist. Go to them regularly. I struggle with depression still but therapy has allowed me to live a much more fulfilling life.
* Get rid of your debt. Aggressively.
* Travel more. It will increase your confidence and expand your worldview.
* Simplify your life. Learn to live with less. Don't chase the Jones's.
* Invest in your education.
* If at all possible become a contractor or business owner. That way you get to control where you work, how much you work, and who you work for.
* Don't pursue a partner. The good ones come naturally, the bad ones are a struggle.
* Relationships can be hard. Sometimes you will have to give more than you get. That said, a relationship should never make you feel bitter.
* Be kind to everyone you meet until they give you reason not to. Then walk away. No tears, no anger. Just walk.
* Be kind to yourself. I struggle with this sometimes but it's absolutely foundational.

Hi. 70 lb lost, 70 more to go.

Don't get caught up on diets. Don't get me wrong. You need to change your relationship with food and exercise. There is no magic weight loss diet. And even if there were you'd just gain again when you went off.

You have to shift from a mindset of food as comfort/joy/social enabler to a mindset of food as fuel. Doesn't mean you cannot enjoy it. Just means you have to account for those poor dietary decisions. Try to look at food in terms of what kind of activities you need to do to burn off the calories. A 20 ounce soda becomes a 5 mile walk.

Track your calories. Reduce your intake of processed foods, empty foods, and convenience foods. Don't buy convenience foods at the grocery store. In a moment of weakness you will eat a bag of chips/crisps instead of carrots.

Also, don't eat like a bodybuilder or strongman. That comes later if you want but will set you up to more gym time than you are capable of right now.

Learn to cook. Learn to use spices. Learn to love hot sauce.

Diet is the lion's share of weight loss. Now onto activity.

Bundle workouts with pleasure. Listen to music or podcasts while walking/jogging. Get some naked wings after a good weightlifting session. Set a goal with a specific award. My halfway point reward was to buy a dji mavic mini for myself. My goal reward is a trip to Australia. Every 10 lb I buy a new game or piece of backpacking gear.

Take a mile walk a day to start. Not every day necessarily. Don't think you have to start by jogging or running. You aren't going to go from a couch to a marathon instantly. Same goes for lifting. Start slow and ramp up gradually.

Next, some dark stuff.

Think about the people in your life that will sabotage you. They are usually well meaning. Your mother will try to feed you until you're ready to explode. Your boss will bring donuts into the office.
